title: State of the Union: Europe Seeks the Ability to Determine Its Own Future
summary: Find out more about State of the Union: Europe Seeks the Ability to Determine Its Own Future, don't miss it.
body_markdown:
This political context coincides with a key institutional moment. The current European legislative term is approaching its midpoint, entering a particularly important phase for transforming the priorities announced at the beginning of the mandate into concrete proposals and, above all, advancing their implementation.


All of this is taking place while Europe faces profound transformations: growing geopolitical tensions, intense technological and global economic competition, and new threats to the security and resilience of its infrastructure.


The central message was clear: Europe wants to strengthen its capacity to determine its own future. To achieve this, it needs a stronger economy, companies capable of growing and competing globally, resilient infrastructure, and reduced external dependencies in strategic areas. However, a more autonomous Europe does not mean a more isolated Europe. On the contrary, von der Leyen advocated expanding and rethinking European partnerships in an international environment increasingly defined by competition between geopolitical blocs.


Canada was the most novel example. The President proposed moving beyond the current CETA trade agreement toward an “Alliance for the Future,” encompassing technology, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, cybersecurity, defence, energy, critical minerals, and economic security. She went even further by suggesting the possibility of Canada becoming the European Union’s first “associate member,” a concept that remains to be defined but reflects the ambition to create new forms of cooperation with strategic partners.


## Competitiveness: Moving from Diagnosis to Execution


Competitiveness received less prominence throughout the speech than many had expected, but it was still present in some of its most significant economic proposals. Von der Leyen herself acknowledged one of the European economy’s main contradictions: Europe possesses a vast market, world-class companies and services, high levels of savings, and a global currency, yet its capital, networks, and purchasing power remain fragmented.


The diagnosis is not new. The Draghi and Letta reports have already identified many of these barriers. The challenge now is to accelerate implementation. Hence the commitment to advance the One Europe, One Market roadmap and complete Single Market reform by the end of 2027. This is accompanied by a particularly strong focus on simplification: speeding up permitting procedures for strategic projects, reducing administrative burdens, and addressing national gold-plating practices. The Commission estimates that the twelve omnibus packages proposed so far could reduce administrative burdens by around €17 billion annually.


For investment-and innovation-intensive sectors such as telecommunications, this debate is especially relevant. Scale, investment, and innovation are closely interconnected: a more integrated market enables companies to grow, strengthen their investment capacity, and accelerate the deployment of new technologies. Reducing fragmentation and simplifying regulation are therefore not merely administrative exercises but essential elements for strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and technological capabilities. However, simplification alone is not enough; the regulatory framework must also create the conditions and incentives necessary to promote investment and innovation.


It was noteworthy, however, that the speech did not include specific references to the telecommunications sector or to the key regulatory initiatives that will shape its future. Nor were there references to the review of EU merger guidelines. Connectivity appeared only indirectly within a broader agenda focused on competitiveness, resilience, and strategic autonomy. For that very reason, the next step will be to translate that ambition into a framework that enables European companies to achieve scale, invest, and innovate, while recognizing the role of advanced and resilient networks as the foundation of Europe’s digital transformation.


## Innovation: Bringing Frontier Technologies into the Real Economy


Innovation also featured prominently. The Commission aims to accelerate the industrial deployment of frontier technologies, particularly artificial intelligence across strategic sectors such as healthcare, transport, agrifood, advanced manufacturing, defence, and space.


Europe’s challenge is no longer simply developing strong technologies, but ensuring that they can be deployed, scaled, and translated into productivity gains. Achieving this requires a complete ecosystem comprising advanced networks, cloud and edge computing infrastructure, data centres, computing capacity, data, talent, and companies capable of investing and scaling.


Connectivity is the essential infrastructure underpinning much of this digital ecosystem. Europe is unlikely to lead in artificial intelligence, advanced industry, or digital services without modern, secure, and resilient networks capable of supporting these technologies and delivering their benefits across society.


## Security and Resilience: Infrastructure for a More Uncertain World


Geopolitics was a recurring theme throughout much of the speech. References to hybrid threats, cybersecurity, space, defence, and critical infrastructure highlight the extent to which economic and technological security have become integral components of the European agenda.


Europe seeks to reduce excessive dependencies in critical raw materials, semiconductors, and essential technologies, diversify suppliers, and strengthen its own capabilities.


This vision of strategic autonomy should not translate into isolation. Technological sovereignty is also about maintaining a genuine capacity to choose: having secure and resilient infrastructure, developing European capabilities, while also ensuring diversified supply chains with sufficient providers and technological alternatives. This approach helps reduce dependencies, reinforce competition, and improve resilience against potential disruptions.


Telecommunications networks form part of this strategic infrastructure. Strengthening their resilience requires a broad approach encompassing cybersecurity, service continuity and availability, the protection of critical infrastructure, and crisis and hybrid-threat response capabilities. This objective should build on existing frameworks and capabilities, avoiding additional regulatory obligations or duplication that could divert resources away from investment and network modernization.


## Protecting Minors and Restoring Digital Trust


The protection of minors featured prominently in the speech, with the announcement of the EU Kids Act, which will primarily strengthen the responsibilities of online platforms in areas such as age verification, addictive features, and safety-by-design requirements.


Telefónica fully supports the objective of creating a safer digital environment for children and adolescents and has been actively engaged in this area for many years. Although the newly announced obligations are mainly directed at platforms, the protection of minors requires engagement from the entire digital ecosystem. As a telecommunications operator, Telefónica contributes through tools and solutions that promote safer and more responsible technology use, as well as through digital education and skills initiatives.


Trust and security are, ultimately, essential conditions for sustainable and inclusive digitalization.


## From Ambition to Execution


In essence, the State of the Union presents a Europe seeking to become more autonomous, resilient, and innovative. Yet it also leaves open a fundamental question: how to translate that ambition into real economic and technological capacity.


Europe must undertake an ambitious reform agenda that addresses the structural factors that have constrained growth and competitiveness. In this context, the proposed Digital Networks Act was presented as the EU’s vehicle for updating the telecommunications regulatory framework with the aim of strengthening the sector’s capacity to invest and innovate. However, aside from the positive proposal on spectrum regulation, the current proposal does not address the sector’s main challenges and lacks meaningful measures and incentives to support investment, innovation, and scale.


Europe has world-class companies, talent, scientific capabilities, and a market of 450 million citizens. The challenge is creating the conditions that allow these strengths to achieve scale.


To achieve this, Europe will need to move more quickly on completing the Single Market and not only simplify regulation but also ensure that the regulatory framework supports the investment, innovation, and scale required to deploy advanced and resilient digital infrastructure. It will also be necessary to build a digital environment in which innovation, security, and trust evolve together.


Legislative proposals with the greatest impact on the telecommunications sector, such as the Digital Networks Act (DNA) and the Cybersecurity Act 2 (CSA2), will provide an opportunity to turn these objectives into reality and ensure a proportionate framework that strengthens competitiveness, investment capacity, and sector resilience.


The next phase of the European agenda will therefore be less about producing new diagnoses and more about execution. Because Europe’s ability to shape its future will depend largely on its capacity to invest, innovate, and compete.
